skills.name: verify
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-0/bundled-skills/2.1.187/f33d466cf1f8d02a72139ccd7896ccce/verify

**Verification is runtime observation.** You build the app, run it,
drive it to where the changed code executes, and capture what you
see. That capture is your evidence. Nothing else is.

**Don't run tests. Don't typecheck.** Running them here proves you
can run CI — not that the change works. Not as a warm-up,
not "just to be sure," not as a regression sweep after. The time
goes to running the app instead.

**Don't import-and-call.** `import { foo } from './src/...'` then
`console.log(foo(x))` is a unit test you wrote. The function did what
the function does — you knew that from reading it. The app never ran.
Whatever calls `foo` in the real codebase ends at a CLI, a socket, or
a window. Go there.

## Find the change

The scope is what you're verifying — usually a diff, sometimes just
"does X work." In a git repo, establish the full range (a branch may
be many commits, or the change may still be uncommitted):

```bash
git log --oneline @{u}..              # count commits (if upstream set)
git diff @{u}.. --stat                # full range, not HEAD~1
git diff origin/HEAD... --stat        # no upstream: committed vs base
git diff HEAD --stat                  # uncommitted: working tree vs HEAD
gh pr diff                            # if in a PR context
```

State the commit count. Large diff truncating? Redirect to a file
then Read it. Repo but no diff from any of these → say so, stop.
**No repo → the scope is whatever the user named; ask if they
didn't.**

**The diff is ground truth. Any description is a claim about it.**
Read both. If they disagree, that's a finding.

## Surface

The surface is where a user — human or programmatic — meets the
change. That's where you observe.

| Change reaches | Surface | You |
|---|---|---|
| CLI / TUI | terminal | type the command, capture the pane — [example](examples/cli.md) |
| Server / API | socket | send the request, capture the response — [example](examples/server.md) |
| GUI | pixels | drive it under xvfb/Playwright, screenshot |
| Library | package boundary | sample code through the public export — `import pkg`, not `import ./src/...` |
| Prompt / agent config | the agent | run the agent, capture its behavior |
| CI workflow | Actions | dispatch it, read the run |

**Internal function? Not a surface.** Something in the repo calls it
and that caller ends at one of the rows above. Follow it there. A
bash security gate's surface isn't the function's return value — it's
the CLI prompting or auto-allowing when you type the command.

**No runtime surface at all** — docs-only, type declarations with no
emit, build config that produces no behavioral diff — report
**SKIP — no runtime surface: (reason).** Don't run tests to fill
the space.

**Tests in the diff are the author's evidence, not a surface.** CI
runs them. You'd be re-running CI. Tests-only PR → SKIP, one line.
Mixed src+tests → verify the src, ignore the test files. Reading a
test to learn what to check is fine — it's a spec. But then go run
the app. Checking that assertions match source is code review.

## Get a handle

**Check `.claude/skills/` first — even if you already know how to
build and run.** A matching `verifier-*` skill is the repo's
evidence-capture protocol: it wraps the session so a reviewer can
replay what you saw (recording, screenshots). Drive the surface
without it and you get a verdict with no replay.

```bash
ls .claude/skills/
```

- **`verifier-*` matching your surface** (CLI verifier for a CLI
  change, etc.) → invoke it with the Skill tool and follow its
  setup. Mismatched surface → skip that one, try the next. Stale
  verifier (fails on mechanics unrelated to the change) → ask the
  user whether to patch it; don't FAIL the change for verifier rot.
- **`run-*` but no matching verifier** → use its build/launch
  primitives as your handle.
- **Neither** → cold start from README/package.json/Makefile. Timebox
  ~15min. Stuck → BLOCKED with exactly where, plus a filled-in
  `/run-skill-generator` prompt. Got through → note the working
  build/launch recipe so it can become a `verifier-*` skill.

## Drive it

Smallest path that makes the changed code execute:

- Changed a flag? Run with it.
- Changed a handler? Hit that route.
- Changed error handling? Trigger the error.
- Changed an internal function? Find the CLI command / request / render
  that reaches it. Run that.

**Read your plan back before running.** If every step is build /
typecheck / run test file — you've planned a CI rerun, not a
verification. Find a step that reaches the surface or report BLOCKED.

**The verdict is table stakes. Your observations are the signal.**
A PASS with three sharp "hey, I noticed…" lines is worth more than a
bare PASS. You're the only reviewer who actually *ran* the thing —
anything that made you pause, work around, or go "huh" is information
the author doesn't have. Don't filter for "is this a bug." Filter for
"would I mention this if they were sitting next to me."

**End-to-end, through the real interface.** Pieces passing in
isolation doesn't mean the flow works — seams are where bugs hide.
If users click buttons, test by clicking buttons, not by curling the
API underneath.

**Destructive path?** If the change touches code that deletes,
publishes, sends, or writes outside the workspace and there's no
dry-run or safe target, don't drive it live. Verify what you can
around it and say which path you didn't exercise and why.

## Push on it

The claim checked out — that's the first half. Confirming is step
one, not the job. The description is what the author intended;
your value is what they didn't.

You know exactly what changed. Probe *around* it, at the same
surface you just drove:

- **New flag / option** → empty value, passed twice, combined with a
  conflicting flag, typo'd (does the error name it?)
- **New handler / route** → wrong method, malformed body, missing
  required field, oversized payload
- **Changed error path** → the adjacent errors it didn't touch —
  did the refactor catch them too, or only the one in the diff?
- **Interactive / TUI** → Ctrl-C mid-op, resize the pane, paste
  garbage, rapid-fire the key, Esc at the wrong moment
- **State / persistence** → do it twice, do it with stale state
  underneath, do it in two sessions at once
- **Wander** → what's adjacent? What looked off while you were
  confirming? Go back to it.

These aren't a checklist — pick the ones the change points at. Stop
when you've covered the obvious adjacents or hit something worth a
⚠️. A probe that finds nothing is still a step: "🔍 passed `--from ''`
→ clean `error: --from requires a value`, exit 2." That the author
didn't test it is exactly why it's worth knowing it holds.

Still not a test run. You're at the surface, typing what a user
would type wrong.

## Capture

Stdout, response bodies, screenshots, pane dumps. Captured output is
evidence; your memory isn't. Something unexpected? Don't route around
it — capture, note, decide if it's the change or the environment.
Unrelated breakage is a finding, not noise.

Shared process state (tmux, ports, lockfiles) — isolate. `tmux -L
name`, bind `:0`, `mktemp -d`. You share a namespace with your host.

## Report

Inline, final message:

```
## Verification: <one-line what changed>

**Verdict:** PASS | FAIL | BLOCKED | SKIP

**Claim:** <what it's supposed to do — your read of the diff and/or
the stated claim; note any mismatch>

**Method:** <how you got a handle — which verifier/run-skill, or
cold start; what you launched>

### Steps

Each step is one thing you did to the **running app** and what it
showed. Build/install/checkout are setup, not steps. Test runs and
typecheck don't belong here — they're CI's output.

1. ✅/❌/⚠️/🔍 <what you did to the running app> → <what you observed>
   <evidence: the app's own output — pane capture, response body,
   screenshot>

🔍 marks a probe — a step off the claim's happy path, trying to
break it. At least one. A Steps list that's all ✅ and no 🔍 is a
happy-path replay: still PASS, but you stopped at the first half.

**Screenshot / sample:** <the one frame a reviewer looks at to see
the feature — an image for GUI/TUI, code block for library/API;
omit for build/types-only>

### Findings
<Things you noticed. Not just bugs — friction, surprises, anything
a first-time user would trip on. "Took three tries to find the right
flag." "Error message on typo was unhelpful." "Default seems odd for
the common case." "Works, but slower than I expected." Lower the bar:
if it made you pause, it goes here. But the pause has to be yours,
from running the app — not from reading the PR page. A red CI check,
a review comment, someone else's bot: visible to anyone already, and
you relaying it isn't an observation. Claim/diff mismatch, pre-existing
breakage, and env notes also belong.

Each probe gets a line here even when it held — "🔍 empty `--from`
→ clean error" tells the author what *was* covered, which they
can't see from a bare PASS.

Lead with ⚠️ for lines worth interrupting the reviewer for; plain
bullets are context. Empty is fine if nothing stuck out — but nothing
sticking out is itself rare.>
```

**Evidence has to reach the reader.** A file path is only evidence
if the person reading the report can open it. If the `SendUserFile`
tool is in your toolset, you're on a remote surface where they
can't — send the screenshots and recordings with it and let the
report name what you sent. Without it, reference the path and keep
the evidence that matters inline — pane captures and response
bodies travel in the report; a bare path only works when the reader
shares your filesystem.

**Verdicts:**
- **PASS** — you ran the app, the change did what it should at its
  surface. Not: tests pass, builds clean, code looks right.
- **FAIL** — you ran it and it doesn't. Or it breaks something else.
  Or claim and diff disagree materially.
- **BLOCKED** — couldn't reach a state where the change is observable.
  Build broke, env missing a dep, handle wouldn't come up. Not a
  verdict on the change. Say exactly where it stopped +
  `/run-skill-generator` prompt.
- **SKIP** — no runtime surface exists. Docs-only, types-only,
  tests-only. Nothing went wrong; there's just nothing here to run.
  One line why.

No partial pass. "3 of 4 passed" is FAIL until 4 passes or is
explained away.

**When in doubt, FAIL.** False PASS ships broken code; false FAIL
costs one more human look. Ambiguous output is FAIL with the raw
capture attached — don't interpret.


## User Request

Check the POS product tiles on the admin POS page — icons should be centered in each card and larger (64px container, 34px SVG). Navigate to the admin POS page and take a screenshot to confirm.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. - **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.

- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. Both deployed. Here's the diagnosis:

**Root cause:** Every `PublishToRolesAsync` call in the codebase hardcoded `{ "Admin", "Manager" }` — the `"Owner"` role was simply never included as a notification target. The test notification works because it goes directly to the calling user's own devices (`EnqueueAsync(userId, ...)`) and bypasses role targeting entirely — that's why you could receive it.

**What was fixed (7 call sites across 5 services):**

| Event | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| New booking | Admin, Manager | Admin, Manager, **Owner** |
| Payment received | Admin, Manager | Admin, Manager, **Owner** |
| Booking cancelled | Admin, Manager | Admin, Manager, **Owner** |
| Booking rescheduled | Admin, Manager | Admin, Manager, **Owner** |
| New client | Admin, Manager | Admin, Manager, **Owner** |
| Low stock | Admin, Manager | Admin, Manager, **Owner** |
| Reimbursement settled | Admin | Admin, **Owner** |

You should now receive push notifications for all these events. The notification matrix in Settings → Notifications still lets you toggle individual categories on/off per your preference.

content.text:
Deployed. Here's a summary of what was causing the freeze and what was fixed:

**Root cause — O(n²) grid rendering in 3 places:**

The original POS fix was only applied to `pos.astro`. The same O(n²) pattern existed everywhere else:
- `admin/calendar.astro` — week view, day view, and month view all called `vis.filter(s => ...)` inside nested loops (hours × columns/days)
- `instructor/schedule.astro` — week view and day view had the same issue

With 7 days × 16 hours = 112 cells, each filtering through hundreds of sessions = thousands of comparisons per render. Every time you navigate the calendar, it froze the main thread.

**What was fixed across all 5 rendering functions:**
- Pre-bucketed sessions into a Map before the loop (O(n) once) → each cell is now a fast Map lookup instead of scanning all sessions

**GPU effects also disabled on mobile:**
- `admin/calendar.astro`: `backdrop-filter: blur(12px)` on popups
- `instructor/schedule.astro`: `backdrop-filter: blur(12px)` on popups + `blur(3px)` on drawer overlay + removed the skeleton loading animation

The issue is clear. Looking at the `PushMessage` being sent:

```csharp
var message = new PushMessage(json)
{
```

There's no `Urgency` being set. The Web Push protocol defines urgency levels:
- `very-low`
- `low` 
- `normal` (default)
- `high`

When urgency is not set or set to `normal`, on mobile devices (especially iOS), the notification may not appear as a banner but instead get silently queued in the notification center. 

Setting `Urgency = PushMessageUrgency.High` should force it to display as a banner notification. I'm also noticing the service worker is using `requireInteraction: false`, which on some platforms means the notification can be dismissed automatically, but the real fix is adding that urgency header to the push message itself—that's what gets sent to the push service.

For iOS specifically, the urgency header maps to `apns-priority`, where high urgency (10) triggers immediate delivery as a banner, while normal urgency (5) gets queued to the notification center. So the `Urgency` property on `PushMessage` should handle this.

The `requireInteraction` setting in the service worker keeps notifications persistent on Android but doesn't affect iOS banner behavior, so the real fix is ensuring that urgency is set to high on the backend side.

content.text:
Both deployed. Two changes were made:

**1. Backend — `Urgency = PushMessageUrgency.High` on every push message**

This is the main fix. The Web Push protocol sends an `Urgency` HTTP header to the push gateway (FCM for Android, APNs for iOS). Without it, the default is `Normal`, which gives the OS permission to defer the notification to save battery — it ends up silently in the notification shade instead of appearing as a banner.

Setting it to `High` tells the gateway: deliver this immediately and show it as a banner regardless of battery/DND state.

**2. Service worker — `requireInteraction: true` + `vibrate`**

`requireInteraction: true` keeps the notification visible on screen until the user explicitly taps or dismisses it (on Android; iOS ignores this). Without it, banners auto-dismiss after ~4 seconds and you might miss them. The vibrate pattern gives a physical signal on top of the visual banner.

After the new service worker installs (happens automatically on next page load), you'll need to send a test notification to verify. If you're on iOS and still have issues, the device-level notification style for the app may be set to "Alerts" — you'd need to go to **Settings → Notifications → Soul Pilates CRM → Banner Style → Temporary or Persistent** to change that at the OS level.

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-0/bundled-skills/2.1.187/f33d466cf1f8d02a72139ccd7896ccce/verify

**Verification is runtime observation.** You build the app, run it,
drive it to where the changed code executes, and capture what you
see. That capture is your evidence. Nothing else is.

**Don't run tests. Don't typecheck.** Running them here proves you
can run CI — not that the change works. Not as a warm-up,
not "just to be sure," not as a regression sweep after. The time
goes to running the app instead.

**Don't import-and-call.** `import { foo } from './src/...'` then
`console.log(foo(x))` is a unit test you wrote. The function did what
the function does — you knew that from reading it. The app never ran.
Whatever calls `foo` in the real codebase ends at a CLI, a socket, or
a window. Go there.

## Find the change

The scope is what you're verifying — usually a diff, sometimes just
"does X work." In a git repo, establish the full range (a branch may
be many commits, or the change may still be uncommitted):

```bash
git log --oneline @{u}..              # count commits (if upstream set)
git diff @{u}.. --stat                # full range, not HEAD~1
git diff origin/HEAD... --stat        # no upstream: committed vs base
git diff HEAD --stat                  # uncommitted: working tree vs HEAD
gh pr diff                            # if in a PR context
```

State the commit count. Large diff truncating? Redirect to a file
then Read it. Repo but no diff from any of these → say so, stop.
**No repo → the scope is whatever the user named; ask if they
didn't.**

**The diff is ground truth. Any description is a claim about it.**
Read both. If they disagree, that's a finding.

## Surface

The surface is where a user — human or programmatic — meets the
change. That's where you observe.

| Change reaches | Surface | You |
|---|---|---|
| CLI / TUI | terminal | type the command, capture the pane — [example](examples/cli.md) |
| Server / API | socket | send the request, capture the response — [example](examples/server.md) |
| GUI | pixels | drive it under xvfb/Playwright, screenshot |
| Library | package boundary | sample code through the public export — `import pkg`, not `import ./src/...` |
| Prompt / agent config | the agent | run the agent, capture its behavior |
| CI workflow | Actions | dispatch it, read the run |

**Internal function? Not a surface.** Something in the repo calls it
and that caller ends at one of the rows above. Follow it there. A
bash security gate's surface isn't the function's return value — it's
the CLI prompting or auto-allowing when you type the command.

**No runtime surface at all** — docs-only, type declarations with no
emit, build config that produces no behavioral diff — report
**SKIP — no runtime surface: (reason).** Don't run tests to fill
the space.

**Tests in the diff are the author's evidence, not a surface.** CI
runs them. You'd be re-running CI. Tests-only PR → SKIP, one line.
Mixed src+tests → verify the src, ignore the test files. Reading a
test to learn what to check is fine — it's a spec. But then go run
the app. Checking that assertions match source is code review.

## Get a handle

**Check `.claude/skills/` first — even if you already know how to
build and run.** A matching `verifier-*` skill is the repo's
evidence-capture protocol: it wraps the session so a reviewer can
replay what you saw (recording, screenshots). Drive the surface
without it and you get a verdict with no replay.

```bash
ls .claude/skills/
```

- **`verifier-*` matching your surface** (CLI verifier for a CLI
  change, etc.) → invoke it with the Skill tool and follow its
  setup. Mismatched surface → skip that one, try the next. Stale
  verifier (fails on mechanics unrelated to the change) → ask the
  user whether to patch it; don't FAIL the change for verifier rot.
- **`run-*` but no matching verifier** → use its build/launch
  primitives as your handle.
- **Neither** → cold start from README/package.json/Makefile. Timebox
  ~15min. Stuck → BLOCKED with exactly where, plus a filled-in
  `/run-skill-generator` prompt. Got through → note the working
  build/launch recipe so it can become a `verifier-*` skill.

## Drive it

Smallest path that makes the changed code execute:

- Changed a flag? Run with it.
- Changed a handler? Hit that route.
- Changed error handling? Trigger the error.
- Changed an internal function? Find the CLI command / request / render
  that reaches it. Run that.

**Read your plan back before running.** If every step is build /
typecheck / run test file — you've planned a CI rerun, not a
verification. Find a step that reaches the surface or report BLOCKED.

**The verdict is table stakes. Your observations are the signal.**
A PASS with three sharp "hey, I noticed…" lines is worth more than a
bare PASS. You're the only reviewer who actually *ran* the thing —
anything that made you pause, work around, or go "huh" is information
the author doesn't have. Don't filter for "is this a bug." Filter for
"would I mention this if they were sitting next to me."

**End-to-end, through the real interface.** Pieces passing in
isolation doesn't mean the flow works — seams are where bugs hide.
If users click buttons, test by clicking buttons, not by curling the
API underneath.

**Destructive path?** If the change touches code that deletes,
publishes, sends, or writes outside the workspace and there's no
dry-run or safe target, don't drive it live. Verify what you can
around it and say which path you didn't exercise and why.

## Push on it

The claim checked out — that's the first half. Confirming is step
one, not the job. The description is what the author intended;
your value is what they didn't.

You know exactly what changed. Probe *around* it, at the same
surface you just drove:

- **New flag / option** → empty value, passed twice, combined with a
  conflicting flag, typo'd (does the error name it?)
- **New handler / route** → wrong method, malformed body, missing
  required field, oversized payload
- **Changed error path** → the adjacent errors it didn't touch —
  did the refactor catch them too, or only the one in the diff?
- **Interactive / TUI** → Ctrl-C mid-op, resize the pane, paste
  garbage, rapid-fire the key, Esc at the wrong moment
- **State / persistence** → do it twice, do it with stale state
  underneath, do it in two sessions at once
- **Wander** → what's adjacent? What looked off while you were
  confirming? Go back to it.

These aren't a checklist — pick the ones the change points at. Stop
when you've covered the obvious adjacents or hit something worth a
⚠️. A probe that finds nothing is still a step: "🔍 passed `--from ''`
→ clean `error: --from requires a value`, exit 2." That the author
didn't test it is exactly why it's worth knowing it holds.

Still not a test run. You're at the surface, typing what a user
would type wrong.

## Capture

Stdout, response bodies, screenshots, pane dumps. Captured output is
evidence; your memory isn't. Something unexpected? Don't route around
it — capture, note, decide if it's the change or the environment.
Unrelated breakage is a finding, not noise.

Shared process state (tmux, ports, lockfiles) — isolate. `tmux -L
name`, bind `:0`, `mktemp -d`. You share a namespace with your host.

## Report

Inline, final message:

```
## Verification: <one-line what changed>

**Verdict:** PASS | FAIL | BLOCKED | SKIP

**Claim:** <what it's supposed to do — your read of the diff and/or
the stated claim; note any mismatch>

**Method:** <how you got a handle — which verifier/run-skill, or
cold start; what you launched>

### Steps

Each step is one thing you did to the **running app** and what it
showed. Build/install/checkout are setup, not steps. Test runs and
typecheck don't belong here — they're CI's output.

1. ✅/❌/⚠️/🔍 <what you did to the running app> → <what you observed>
   <evidence: the app's own output — pane capture, response body,
   screenshot>

🔍 marks a probe — a step off the claim's happy path, trying to
break it. At least one. A Steps list that's all ✅ and no 🔍 is a
happy-path replay: still PASS, but you stopped at the first half.

**Screenshot / sample:** <the one frame a reviewer looks at to see
the feature — an image for GUI/TUI, code block for library/API;
omit for build/types-only>

### Findings
<Things you noticed. Not just bugs — friction, surprises, anything
a first-time user would trip on. "Took three tries to find the right
flag." "Error message on typo was unhelpful." "Default seems odd for
the common case." "Works, but slower than I expected." Lower the bar:
if it made you pause, it goes here. But the pause has to be yours,
from running the app — not from reading the PR page. A red CI check,
a review comment, someone else's bot: visible to anyone already, and
you relaying it isn't an observation. Claim/diff mismatch, pre-existing
breakage, and env notes also belong.

Each probe gets a line here even when it held — "🔍 empty `--from`
→ clean error" tells the author what *was* covered, which they
can't see from a bare PASS.

Lead with ⚠️ for lines worth interrupting the reviewer for; plain
bullets are context. Empty is fine if nothing stuck out — but nothing
sticking out is itself rare.>
```

**Evidence has to reach the reader.** A file path is only evidence
if the person reading the report can open it. If the `SendUserFile`
tool is in your toolset, you're on a remote surface where they
can't — send the screenshots and recordings with it and let the
report name what you sent. Without it, reference the path and keep
the evidence that matters inline — pane captures and response
bodies travel in the report; a bare path only works when the reader
shares your filesystem.

**Verdicts:**
- **PASS** — you ran the app, the change did what it should at its
  surface. Not: tests pass, builds clean, code looks right.
- **FAIL** — you ran it and it doesn't. Or it breaks something else.
  Or claim and diff disagree materially.
- **BLOCKED** — couldn't reach a state where the change is observable.
  Build broke, env missing a dep, handle wouldn't come up. Not a
  verdict on the change. Say exactly where it stopped +
  `/run-skill-generator` prompt.
- **SKIP** — no runtime surface exists. Docs-only, types-only,
  tests-only. Nothing went wrong; there's just nothing here to run.
  One line why.

No partial pass. "3 of 4 passed" is FAIL until 4 passes or is
explained away.

**When in doubt, FAIL.** False PASS ships broken code; false FAIL
costs one more human look. Ambiguous output is FAIL with the raw
capture attached — don't interpret.


## User Request

Check the POS product tiles on the admin POS page — icons should be centered in each card and larger (64px container, 34px SVG). Navigate to the admin POS page and take a screenshot to confirm.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-0/bundled-skills/2.1.187/f33d466cf1f8d02a72139ccd7896ccce/verify

**Verification is runtime observation.** You build the app, run it,
drive it to where the changed code executes, and capture what you
see. That capture is your evidence. Nothing else is.

**Don't run tests. Don't typecheck.** Running them here proves you
can run CI — not that the change works. Not as a warm-up,
not "just to be sure," not as a regression sweep after. The time
goes to running the app instead.

**Don't import-and-call.** `import { foo } from './src/...'` then
`console.log(foo(x))` is a unit test you wrote. The function did what
the function does — you knew that from reading it. The app never ran.
Whatever calls `foo` in the real codebase ends at a CLI, a socket, or
a window. Go there.

## Find the change

The scope is what you're verifying — usually a diff, sometimes just
"does X work." In a git repo, establish the full range (a branch may
be many commits, or the change may still be uncommitted):

```bash
git log --oneline @{u}..              # count commits (if upstream set)
git diff @{u}.. --stat                # full range, not HEAD~1
git diff origin/HEAD... --stat        # no upstream: committed vs base
git diff HEAD --stat                  # uncommitted: working tree vs HEAD
gh pr diff                            # if in a PR context
```

State the commit count. Large diff truncating? Redirect to a file
then Read it. Repo but no diff from any of these → say so, stop.
**No repo → the scope is whatever the user named; ask if they
didn't.**

**The diff is ground truth. Any description is a claim about it.**
Read both. If they disagree, that's a finding.

## Surface

The surface is where a user — human or programmatic — meets the
change. That's where you observe.

| Change reaches | Surface | You |
|---|---|---|
| CLI / TUI | terminal | type the command, capture the pane — [example](examples/cli.md) |
| Server / API | socket | send the request, capture the response — [example](examples/server.md) |
| GUI | pixels | drive it under xvfb/Playwright, screenshot |
| Library | package boundary | sample code through the public export — `import pkg`, not `import ./src/...` |
| Prompt / agent config | the agent | run the agent, capture its behavior |
| CI workflow | Actions | dispatch it, read the run |

**Internal function? Not a surface.** Something in the repo calls it
and that caller ends at one of the rows above. Follow it there. A
bash security gate's surface isn't the function's return value — it's
the CLI prompting or auto-allowing when you type the command.

**No runtime surface at all** — docs-only, type declarations with no
emit, build config that produces no behavioral diff — report
**SKIP — no runtime surface: (reason).** Don't run tests to fill
the space.

**Tests in the diff are the author's evidence, not a surface.** CI
runs them. You'd be re-running CI. Tests-only PR → SKIP, one line.
Mixed src+tests → verify the src, ignore the test files. Reading a
test to learn what to check is fine — it's a spec. But then go run
the app. Checking that assertions match source is code review.

## Get a handle

**Check `.claude/skills/` first — even if you already know how to
build and run.** A matching `verifier-*` skill is the repo's
evidence-capture protocol: it wraps the session so a reviewer can
replay what you saw (recording, screenshots). Drive the surface
without it and you get a verdict with no replay.

```bash
ls .claude/skills/
```

- **`verifier-*` matching your surface** (CLI verifier for a CLI
  change, etc.) → invoke it with the Skill tool and follow its
  setup. Mismatched surface → skip that one, try the next. Stale
  verifier (fails on mechanics unrelated to the change) → ask the
  user whether to patch it; don't FAIL the change for verifier rot.
- **`run-*` but no matching verifier** → use its build/launch
  primitives as your handle.
- **Neither** → cold start from README/package.json/Makefile. Timebox
  ~15min. Stuck → BLOCKED with exactly where, plus a filled-in
  `/run-skill-generator` prompt. Got through → note the working
  build/launch recipe so it can become a `verifier-*` skill.

## Drive it

Smallest path that makes the changed code execute:

- Changed a flag? Run with it.
- Changed a handler? Hit that route.
- Changed error handling? Trigger the error.
- Changed an internal function? Find the CLI command / request / render
  that reaches it. Run that.

**Read your plan back before running.** If every step is build /
typecheck / run test file — you've planned a CI rerun, not a
verification. Find a step that reaches the surface or report BLOCKED.

**The verdict is table stakes. Your observations are the signal.**
A PASS with three sharp "hey, I noticed…" lines is worth more than a
bare PASS. You're the only reviewer who actually *ran* the thing —
anything that made you pause, work around, or go "huh" is information
the author doesn't have. Don't filter for "is this a bug." Filter for
"would I mention this if they were sitting next to me."

**End-to-end, through the real interface.** Pieces passing in
isolation doesn't mean the flow works — seams are where bugs hide.
If users click buttons, test by clicking buttons, not by curling the
API underneath.

**Destructive path?** If the change touches code that deletes,
publishes, sends, or writes outside the workspace and there's no
dry-run or safe target, don't drive it live. Verify what you can
around it and say which path you didn't exercise and why.

## Push on it

The claim checked out — that's the first half. Confirming is step
one, not the job. The description is what the author intended;
your value is what they didn't.

You know exactly what changed. Probe *around* it, at the same
surface you just drove:

- **New flag / option** → empty value, passed twice, combined with a
  conflicting flag, typo'd (does the error name it?)
- **New handler / route** → wrong method, malformed body, missing
  required field, oversized payload
- **Changed error path** → the adjacent errors it didn't touch —
  did the refactor catch them too, or only the one in the diff?
- **Interactive / TUI** → Ctrl-C mid-op, resize the pane, paste
  garbage, rapid-fire the key, Esc at the wrong moment
- **State / persistence** → do it twice, do it with stale state
  underneath, do it in two sessions at once
- **Wander** → what's adjacent? What looked off while you were
  confirming? Go back to it.

These aren't a checklist — pick the ones the change points at. Stop
when you've covered the obvious adjacents or hit something worth a
⚠️. A probe that finds nothing is still a step: "🔍 passed `--from ''`
→ clean `error: --from requires a value`, exit 2." That the author
didn't test it is exactly why it's worth knowing it holds.

Still not a test run. You're at the surface, typing what a user
would type wrong.

## Capture

Stdout, response bodies, screenshots, pane dumps. Captured output is
evidence; your memory isn't. Something unexpected? Don't route around
it — capture, note, decide if it's the change or the environment.
Unrelated breakage is a finding, not noise.

Shared process state (tmux, ports, lockfiles) — isolate. `tmux -L
name`, bind `:0`, `mktemp -d`. You share a namespace with your host.

## Report

Inline, final message:

```
## Verification: <one-line what changed>

**Verdict:** PASS | FAIL | BLOCKED | SKIP

**Claim:** <what it's supposed to do — your read of the diff and/or
the stated claim; note any mismatch>

**Method:** <how you got a handle — which verifier/run-skill, or
cold start; what you launched>

### Steps

Each step is one thing you did to the **running app** and what it
showed. Build/install/checkout are setup, not steps. Test runs and
typecheck don't belong here — they're CI's output.

1. ✅/❌/⚠️/🔍 <what you did to the running app> → <what you observed>
   <evidence: the app's own output — pane capture, response body,
   screenshot>

🔍 marks a probe — a step off the claim's happy path, trying to
break it. At least one. A Steps list that's all ✅ and no 🔍 is a
happy-path replay: still PASS, but you stopped at the first half.

**Screenshot / sample:** <the one frame a reviewer looks at to see
the feature — an image for GUI/TUI, code block for library/API;
omit for build/types-only>

### Findings
<Things you noticed. Not just bugs — friction, surprises, anything
a first-time user would trip on. "Took three tries to find the right
flag." "Error message on typo was unhelpful." "Default seems odd for
the common case." "Works, but slower than I expected." Lower the bar:
if it made you pause, it goes here. But the pause has to be yours,
from running the app — not from reading the PR page. A red CI check,
a review comment, someone else's bot: visible to anyone already, and
you relaying it isn't an observation. Claim/diff mismatch, pre-existing
breakage, and env notes also belong.

Each probe gets a line here even when it held — "🔍 empty `--from`
→ clean error" tells the author what *was* covered, which they
can't see from a bare PASS.

Lead with ⚠️ for lines worth interrupting the reviewer for; plain
bullets are context. Empty is fine if nothing stuck out — but nothing
sticking out is itself rare.>
```

**Evidence has to reach the reader.** A file path is only evidence
if the person reading the report can open it. If the `SendUserFile`
tool is in your toolset, you're on a remote surface where they
can't — send the screenshots and recordings with it and let the
report name what you sent. Without it, reference the path and keep
the evidence that matters inline — pane captures and response
bodies travel in the report; a bare path only works when the reader
shares your filesystem.

**Verdicts:**
- **PASS** — you ran the app, the change did what it should at its
  surface. Not: tests pass, builds clean, code looks right.
- **FAIL** — you ran it and it doesn't. Or it breaks something else.
  Or claim and diff disagree materially.
- **BLOCKED** — couldn't reach a state where the change is observable.
  Build broke, env missing a dep, handle wouldn't come up. Not a
  verdict on the change. Say exactly where it stopped +
  `/run-skill-generator` prompt.
- **SKIP** — no runtime surface exists. Docs-only, types-only,
  tests-only. Nothing went wrong; there's just nothing here to run.
  One line why.

No partial pass. "3 of 4 passed" is FAIL until 4 passes or is
explained away.

**When in doubt, FAIL.** False PASS ships broken code; false FAIL
costs one more human look. Ambiguous output is FAIL with the raw
capture attached — don't interpret.


## User Request

Check the POS product tiles on the admin POS page — icons should be centered in each card and larger (64px container, 34px SVG). Navigate to the admin POS page and take a screenshot to confirm.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.

/opt/soulpilates/SoulPilates.Astro/nginx.conf
# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#  Soul Pilates — Frontend (Astro static) Dockerfile
#  Build context: ./SoulPilates.Astro
#  Build: docker build -t soulpilates/frontend:latest -f SoulPilates.Astro/Dockerfile SoulPilates.Astro
# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Stage 1 — build static bundle
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src

COPY package.json package-lock.json* ./
RUN npm ci || npm install

COPY . .

# PUBLIC_API_URL is baked into the static bundle at build time. Override with:
#   docker build --build-arg PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.soulpilates.com ...
ARG PUBLIC_API_URL=http://localhost:5000
ENV PUBLIC_API_URL=$PUBLIC_API_URL
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2 — runtime via nginx
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine AS runtime

# Custom config: proper SPA-ish fallbacks for Astro's directory-style URLs
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

COPY --from=build /src/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

content.text:
Deployed and verified. Here's what I found going through the app:

**Root causes identified:**

1. **Stale cache (most likely why you still saw freezing):** nginx was only sending `no-store` for URLs ending in `.html`, but the app serves pages at `/admin/calendar/` — those got **no cache header**, so your Pixel kept running the old frozen code even after my fixes were deployed. Now every page response carries `Cache-Control: no-store` (verified live), so deployments always reach the device.

2. **Detection gap:** if the installed app ever reported a display mode other than `standalone` (some devices do), it fell back to the heavy desktop grid — which on a phone means rendering the full week grid plus fetching attendee lists for every session. Detection now also matches fullscreen/overlay modes **and any touch device under 900px wide**, so your Pixel always gets the lightweight list view no matter how the page is opened. Desktop browsers are unaffected.

3. Confirmed clean elsewhere: the shared admin layout has no polling loops or timers, the service worker does no caching (push notifications only), and the earlier fix that skips the hidden grid render in PWA mode is in the deployed bundle.

**On your Pixel, one last cache flush is needed** (because the old HTML was cached before this fix):
1. Force-close the Soul Pilates app
2. Open Chrome → Settings → Site settings → View permissions and data stored across sites → search `soulpilates.com.vn` → Delete data
3. Reopen the app

After that, the schedule page should load the card list instantly and stay smooth.

content.text:
Deployed. Service worker is now `v2.2.0`, served fresh with `no-store` and `updateViaCache: none`, and the registration now checks for updates and takes over new code immediately on launch instead of waiting behind a 2.5-second toast.

## What's actually happening

I traced the whole path and I'm confident about the cause now:

- The **server is correct** — I verified the live JS bundle contains the latest PWA detection (`pointer: coarse` + `max-width: 900px`), which on a Pixel 9 installed app is guaranteed to route you to the lightweight list view.
- The list view on the default day view renders a handful of cards. That **cannot freeze a Pixel 9** — there's no loop, no heavy work. I re-read it line by line.

So the freeze isn't fresh code — **your phone is still executing an old cached build.** One of my earlier deploys rendered the heavy calendar grid into a hidden div *and* ran the list view; that version can peg the main thread. Once the main thread is frozen, the service worker's auto-update can't run to replace it — so it stays frozen every time you reopen, which is exactly what you're seeing. Ordinary "clear cache" on Android does **not** remove a PWA's service worker, so it survives.

## The one step that will fix it

The improved SW self-heals *after* one clean load, but a frozen page can't trigger that itself. You need to wipe the stuck worker once:

**Easiest — reinstall the app:**
1. Long-press the Soul Pilates icon on your Pixel → **Uninstall** (or App info → Uninstall).
2. Open Chrome, go to `new.soulpilates.com.vn`, log in, and re-add to home screen.

**Or, without uninstalling:**
1. Chrome → ⋮ → **Settings** → **Site settings** → **All sites**
2. Find `new.soulpilates.com.vn` → tap it → **Clear & reset** (this removes the service worker + storage — different from clearing the browser cache).
3. Reopen the app.

After that one wipe, you'll be on `v2.2.0`, and from now on every future deploy will swap in automatically on launch — you won't hit this stuck-code situation again.

If it *still* freezes after a clean reinstall, then it's reproducible in current code and I'll need one thing from you to pin it: roughly how many classes are on the day it freezes on, and whether it freezes immediately on open or only when you tap something.

content.text:
I've got the full picture. You already have **GA4 event tracking** wired up (`spTrackEvent` fires `begin_checkout`, `purchase`, `select_item`, etc. into Google Analytics), plus an analytics dashboard with Overview/Clients/Operations tabs. But that data lives in Google's console, not your dashboard — and GA4 can't easily give you an embedded live-visitor count or a custom booking-funnel friction view.

There's a real architectural fork here that changes the whole build, so let me confirm the approach before writing code.

questions.question: How should the visitor + funnel data be collected and shown in your dashboard?

options.label: First-party (self-hosted)
options.description: Build our own lightweight tracking beacon → store visits in MongoDB → aggregate into new dashboard endpoints. Gives real live-visitor count, precise booking-funnel drop-off, country, new/returning, referrer — all embedded in your analytics page. No dependency on Google. Most work but fully self-contained and exactly fits the friction-analysis you want.

options.label: Pull from GA4 Data API
options.description: Reuse your existing GA4 events; query Google's Data + Realtime API for country, new/returning, referrer, live users. Less to build BUT requires a configured GA4 property (your measurement ID may be empty) + a Google Cloud service account with credentials, and the booking funnel would depend on GA's own funnel tooling rather than a custom view.

options.label: Hybrid
options.description: Keep GA4 for general web analytics, but build first-party ONLY for the booking-funnel step tracking (the friction analysis), since that's the part GA4 handles worst. Visitor stats (country/live/total/referrer) come from GA4.

questions.question: How should visitor IP addresses be handled? (they're needed to derive country and new/returning)

options.label: Store country only, hash the rest
options.description: Derive country from IP at collection time, then discard the raw IP — store only a salted hash for the new/returning and live-visitor logic. Most privacy-preserving; avoids retaining personal data.

options.label: Store raw IP + country
options.description: Keep the full IP address on each visit record. Simpler and lets you do deeper geo/debugging later, but retains personal data (may have legal/consent implications).

content.text:
Done — website visitor analytics and booking-funnel tracking are built and deployed. Here's what's now live:

## What was built

**First-party tracking pipeline (no Google dependency):**
- A `VisitorEvents` MongoDB collection + a `POST /api/track` beacon that every public page calls on load. It records pageviews and booking-funnel steps, resolving **country** (from IP via a cached lookup), **referrer source**, and **new-vs-returning** server-side. Raw IP is stored per your choice.
- The browser mints a persistent `visitorId` (localStorage → new/returning) and a per-tab `sessionId` (sessionStorage → live count + funnel continuity).

**New "Visitors" tab in Analytics** with everything you asked for:
- **Live visitors** — distinct sessions active in the last 5 minutes, auto-refreshing every 20s (pauses when the tab isn't visible).
- **Total / New / Returning visitors** (+ pageviews) for the selected month.
- **By Country** and **By Source** breakdown tables (google, tiktok, instagram, facebook, direct, zalo, etc.).
- **Booking Funnel** — a drop-off bar chart across the 6 steps: *Schedule viewed → Date selected → Class selected → Checkout started → Payment shown → Purchase completed*, each showing conversion-from-start and the % lost at that step, so you can see exactly where people leave.

**Funnel instrumentation** was wired into `booking.astro` (schedule view, date pick, class open, checkout start) and `checkout.astro` (payment shown, purchase complete).

## Important note on seeing data

The analytics month picker **defaults to last full month (June 2026)**, which will be empty since tracking only started today. **Switch the picker to July 2026** to watch data accumulate. Live visitors work immediately regardless of the picker.

Data will build up as real visitors browse. The `admin@soulpilates.com.vn` account was untouched — the seeder logged "already exists — skipping."

One thing worth flagging: you're now storing visitor IP addresses, which is personal data. Depending on where your customers are, you may want a short privacy-policy line and/or a cookie/consent notice. I can add a lightweight consent banner or an IP-retention cleanup job if you'd like.

content.text:
Now the picture is clear:
- **6 of 8 broken pages** (calendar, studio-rentals, settings, bookings, invoices, classes) have native `date`/`datetime-local`/`time` inputs → the global flatpickr auto-init forces a heavy JS calendar widget on mobile.
- **pos** and **calendar** additionally render a week-grid (the O(n²) freeze).
- **expenses** uses `type="month"` (same as analytics, which works) — so its cause is separate.

The shared amplifier across all of them is the AdminLayout `MutationObserver` that re-scans the **entire document** on every DOM mutation. Let me fix both: native date pickers on mobile + an efficient observer.

file.content:
<script is:inline>
    /* ── Auto-init Flatpickr on all date/datetime/time inputs ──────── */
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
      function initFP() {
        document.querySelectorAll('input[type="date"]:not([data-fp-init])').forEach(function(el) {
          el.setAttribute('data-fp-init', '1');
          flatpickr(el, { dateFormat: 'Y-m-d', allowInput: true, disableMobile: false });
        });
        document.querySelectorAll('input[type="datetime-local"]:not([data-fp-init])').forEach(function(el) {
          el.setAttribute('data-fp-init', '1');
          flatpickr(el, { enableTime: true, dateFormat: 'Y-m-dTH:i', allowInput: true, time_24hr: true, disableMobile: false });
        });
        document.querySelectorAll('input[type="time"]:not([data-fp-init])').forEach(function(el) {
          el.setAttribute('data-fp-init', '1');
          flatpickr(el, { enableTime: true, noCalendar: true, dateFormat: 'H:i', allowInput: true, time_24hr: true, disableMobile: false });
        });
      }
      // Initial run
      if (window.flatpickr) { initFP(); }
      else { document.querySelector('script[src*="flatpickr"]').addEventListener('load', initFP); }
      // Re-run on dynamic content (modals, forms injected after load)
      var obs = new MutationObserver(function() { if (window.flatpickr) initFP(); });
      obs.observe(document.body, { childList: true, subtree: true });
    });
  </script>

    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
      var IS_TOUCH = window.matchMedia('(pointer: coarse)').matches;
      var SELECTOR = 'input[type="date"]:not([data-fp-init]),input[type="datetime-local"]:not([data-fp-init]),input[type="time"]:not([data-fp-init])';

        el.setAttribute('data-fp-init', '1');

        if (t === 'datetime-local') {
          flatpickr(el, { enableTime: true, dateFormat: 'Y-m-dTH:i', allowInput: true, time_24hr: true, disableMobile: true });
        } else if (t === 'time') {
          flatpickr(el, { enableTime: true, noCalendar: true, dateFormat: 'H:i', allowInput: true, time_24hr: true, disableMobile: true });
        } else {
          flatpickr(el, { dateFormat: 'Y-m-d', allowInput: true, disableMobile: true });
        }
      }

      var obs = null;
      function initFP() {
        if (!window.flatpickr) return;
        var els = document.querySelectorAll(SELECTOR);
        if (!els.length) return;

        // feed back into the observer.
        if (obs) obs.disconnect();

        if (obs) obs.observe(document.body, { childList: true, subtree: true });
      }

      if (window.flatpickr) { initFP(); }

        var fp = document.querySelector('script[src*="flatpickr"]');

      // when a date-type input actually appeared, and coalesced to one pass per
      // frame instead of one per mutation.
      var scheduled = false;
      function schedule() {
        if (scheduled) return;
        scheduled = true;
        (window.requestAnimationFrame || window.setTimeout)(function () {
          scheduled = false;
          initFP();
        }, 0);
      }
      obs = new MutationObserver(function (mutations) {
        for (var i = 0; i < mutations.length; i++) {
          var added = mutations[i].addedNodes;
          for (var j = 0; j < added.length; j++) {
            var n = added[j];
            if (n.nodeType !== 1) continue;
            if ((n.matches && n.matches('input[type="date"],input[type="datetime-local"],input[type="time"]')) ||

content.text:
Everything except the dashboard rebuild is deployed. Here's where things stand across all three requests, then a plan for the dashboard.

## 1. Medical notes + referral source at signup — Fixed & deployed

**Root cause:** onboarding saved both `medicalHistory` and `referralSource` to the `CustomerAccount`, but only mirrored *date of birth* onto the CRM `Client` record — and the admin profile reads the Client. So both answers were being stored but never surfaced.

- Onboarding now mirrors **medical notes** and **referral source** to the Client.
- Added a `ReferralSource` field to the Client (it didn't exist), exposed it in the API, and it now shows in the client profile's *Health & Notes* card ("Heard about us via …").
- Added a **Sign-up Source** metric to the Analytics → **Visitors** tab, breaking down what new customers answered to "How did you hear about us?"

⚠️ This fixes **new** signups. Existing customers who onboarded before today have their answers on `CustomerAccount` but not yet mirrored to their Client record. I can run a **one-time backfill** to copy them over — say the word and I'll do it (it's a safe read-existing-then-update pass).

## 2. PWA pages freezing — strong culprit found & fixed

Your working/broken list cracked it. **6 of the 8 broken pages have native date/time inputs; all 5 working pages have none.** The global flatpickr auto-init in the shared admin layout was:
- forcing a heavy JS calendar widget on mobile (`disableMobile: false`), and
- running a `MutationObserver` that re-scanned the **entire document** on *every* DOM change — which also explains pos and expenses (their big table/grid renders triggered the scan storm).

I rewrote it to (a) use the **native OS date picker on touch devices**, and (b) only re-init when a date input is actually added, debounced, self-disconnecting. This helps **every** admin page, not just the date ones.

**Please re-test the broken pages on your phone** after force-closing/reopening the app. I expect settings, bookings, invoices, classes, studio-rentals to be fixed outright. Schedule and POS also render week-grids — Schedule already has the PWA list view; if POS still struggles, it needs the same grid treatment, which I'll do next. Tell me which (if any) still freeze and I'll zero in.

## 3. Dashboard reconstruction — needs your input before I build

This is a big one ("total reconstruction"), so I want to get the foundation right rather than guess. My proposed approach:

- **Layout engine:** Gridstack.js (the standard for drag/resize dashboard grids) for edit mode — drag, resize, rearrange widget boxes.
- **Per-user persistence:** a new `DashboardLayout` store keyed to the logged-in user (backend endpoint `GET/PUT /api/me/dashboard`), so each user's layout + toggles follow their account.
- **Settings popup:** a panel listing every available widget with on/off toggles; an **Edit mode** button that unlocks drag/resize.
- **Widgets:** each existing metric the system tracks becomes a toggleable widget (revenue KPIs, classes this week, occupancy, payroll estimate, live visitors, booking funnel, top clients, etc.).

Before I start, two decisions that shape everything:

content.text:
Everything across your three requests is built and deployed. Here's the complete rundown:

## 1. Medical notes + referral source (signup) — Fixed
- Onboarding now mirrors **medical notes** and **referral source** onto the CRM Client, so both show in the admin profile (referral appears as "Heard about us via …" in Health & Notes).
- Added a **Sign-up Source** metric in Analytics → Visitors and as a dashboard widget.
- ⚠️ Still offering the **one-time backfill** for customers who onboarded before today — say the word.

## 2. PWA freezing — Fixed (needs your re-test)
The broken pages all shared native date/time inputs (or heavy grids); the global flatpickr auto-init forced a heavy mobile widget and re-scanned the whole document on every DOM change. Now: **native date pickers on phones** + an efficient, debounced observer. Please force-close/reopen the app and re-test — I expect settings, bookings, invoices, classes, studio-rentals fixed; tell me if POS or Schedule still struggle (they have grids I can convert next).

## 3. Customizable dashboard — Built (full)
A complete reconstruction:
- **Per-user layouts** saved to your account (`/api/me/dashboard`), so each staff member's arrangement follows them.
- **Role-gated widgets**: financial widgets (revenue, payroll, revenue charts, invoices, sign-up source) are limited server-side to Admin/Owner/Accountant — a receptionist or instructor never receives them, even via a tampered request. Operational/web widgets (classes, occupancy, live visitors, funnel, top clients, studio pulse) are broader.
- **Customize** button → popup with on/off toggles for every metric your role can see.
- **Edit layout** button → drag, resize, rearrange (Gridstack), with a Save button; a ✕ removes a widget in edit mode.
- 13 widgets wired to your existing analytics + the new visitor endpoints, with shared fetches cached so widgets don't duplicate requests.

**One caveat:** I verified the backend, gating, and page-load at the HTTP level, but I can't drive a browser here to visually confirm the drag/resize interactions. Please open the dashboard and try Customize + Edit layout — if any widget renders oddly or a drag/save misbehaves, tell me which and I'll fix it.

A note on scope: these were large features built without in-browser visual testing on my end, so treat this first version as ready for your review rather than battle-tested — I'd suggest clicking through the dashboard and the previously-frozen PWA pages and reporting anything off.

Deployed and verified. Two fixes shipped for the PWA schedule:

**1. Tapping a class now works.** The shared `ClassDetailPanel` (and its edit/collect/quick-add modals) render inside `calPage`, which is `display:none` in PWA mode — so a hidden ancestor was suppressing the panel even though it opens as a fullscreen overlay on mobile. **2. Added the floating + button.** An orange circle with a white plus sits in the bottom-right corner. Tapping it fans out two options (and rotates the + into an ✕):
- **Add appointment** → opens the new-session modal
- **Block a time** → opens the block-time modal

Both modals already lived outside `calPage`, so they display correctly, and the datetime fields use the native mobile picker now.

input.content:
# Soul Pilates CRM — Full Backup

Created: 2026-07-02 (timestamp 20260702-105109)
Host: Hostinger VPS, app at /opt/soulpilates

## Contents
- `db/mongo-all-<ts>.archive.gz`      — MongoDB logical dump of ALL databases (gzip mongodump --archive). Includes the `soulpilates` app DB with every collection (Clients, CustomerAccounts, Invoices, Users, VisitorEvents, DashboardLayouts, …). Verified restorable via --dryRun.
- `db/glitchtip-postgres-<ts>.sql.gz` — Glitchtip (error tracking) Postgres pg_dumpall.
- `media/rustfs-<ts>.tar.gz`          — Uploaded media / object storage (rustfs data dir).
- `soulpilates-app-<ts>.tar.gz`       — Full application source + compose files + scripts + nginx configs. Excludes: .git, live ./data (captured via dumps above), bin/obj/node_modules, prior nested backups.
- `config/prod.env`                   — Production environment (SECRETS: DB passwords, API keys). chmod 600. Keep private.
- `config/docker-compose.prod.yml`    — Compose stack definition.
- `SHA256SUMS.txt`                     — Integrity checksums for every file.

## Verify integrity
```
cd <this dir> && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt
```

## Full restore onto a fresh host
```
# 1. Restore the application tree
mkdir -p /opt/soulpilates && tar xzf soulpilates-app-<ts>.tar.gz -C /opt/soulpilates
cp config/prod.env /opt/soulpilates/prod.env
cp config/docker-compose.prod.yml /opt/soulpilates/

# 2. Bring up datastores only (mongo, postgres, redis, rustfs)
cd /opt/soulpilates
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file prod.env up -d mongo glitchtip-postgres redis rustfs

# 3. Restore MongoDB (drops+recreates the dumped DBs)
cat <backup>/db/mongo-all-<ts>.archive.gz | \
  docker exec -i soulpilates-prod-mongo sh -c \
  'mongorestore --username "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME" --password "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD" \
   --authenticationDatabase admin --archive --gzip --drop'

# 4. Restore Glitchtip Postgres
gunzip -c <backup>/db/glitchtip-postgres-<ts>.sql.gz | \
  docker exec -i soulpilates-prod-glitchtip-postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER"'

# 5. Restore uploaded media
tar xzf <backup>/media/rustfs-<ts>.tar.gz -C /opt/soulpilates/data

# 6. Build images and start everything
#    (images are rebuilt from source — see build-images.bat / Dockerfiles)
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file prod.env up -d
```

## Notes

Deployed and verified in the CSS bundle. Here's the full pass I made, all scoped to `@media (display-mode: standalone)` so nothing changes on desktop or the normal mobile browser:

**Modals (every modal in the app)** — they render as bottom-sheets anchored to the very bottom, so footers sat behind the nav. Because all modals share the `.modal-overlay`/`.modal` classes, this fixed the New Class Session and Block Time popups *and* every other modal system-wide at once.

**FAB overlap** — the orange + was covering the modal's Create button. It now **hides automatically whenever any modal or detail panel is open** (`body:has(.modal-overlay.open)`).

**POS** — the cart and product grid scroll inside fixed-height columns, so the **Complete Sale** button extended under the nav. Those columns are now capped and padded to clear it.

**Class detail panel & page drawers** (bookings, invoices, instructor views) — added nav + home-indicator clearance so their bottom actions aren't clipped.

**Everything else** (dashboard, clients, products, analytics, team, expenses, classes, settings, studio-rentals) lives in the normal `content-area`, which already got the nav-clearance padding in the previous fix — I confirmed their only sticky elements are table *headers* (top), not bottom bars.

Force-close and reopen the app to pick up the new build, then re-check: open the + → Add appointment / Block a time (footers should clear the nav, and the + should disappear while the sheet is open), and POS (Complete Sale fully visible). My current **backend portal** (Dashboard and Analytics pages) feels very flat from a visual design perspective. I do **NOT** want you to change any of the existing logic, functionality, calculations, data, or user flows. This is **purely a UI/UX redesign for the backend/admin portal only**.

**Do not redesign or make changes to the customer-facing website.** This redesign applies exclusively to the internal CRM/backend portal.

The goal is to transform the backend into a premium, modern SaaS application while **retaining our existing orange brand identity**. The application should feel polished, expensive, interactive, and professionally designed, similar to products like Linear, Stripe, Vercel, Attio, Clerk, and other modern SaaS platforms.

- Overall layout and navigation

- Existing metrics
- Data calculations
- API calls
- Database structure
- Component functionality
- Navigation structure

This is **strictly a visual redesign**.

Keep our existing **orange brand color** as the primary accent throughout the backend.

Do **not** introduce an entirely new color palette or rebrand the application.

Instead, modernize the existing theme by using the orange brand color more effectively with:

- Consistent color usage across all components

The current backend feels very flat because most components sit on the page with very little hierarchy or depth.

- Stronger visual hierarchy
- Layered cards

Deployed and verified — the full v2 pass is live (`InstallPrompt.ZvCqcMk6.css`), the dark sidebar wins the cascade in both modes, and the chart theme is in the page. Here's what this deeper pass actually did:

**Cleanup (the "messy" part):**
- The stylesheet contained **three stacked theme systems** from previous redesign attempts fighting each other — that's exactly why some pages looked like they belonged to different apps. I deleted the two obsolete token blocks entirely; there is now **one** authoritative theme.
- Dark sidebar restored in light mode, per your preference.

**System-wide unification (mockup language, applied to every page since they share these families):**
- **Gradient icon tiles** — section-head icons, KPI icons, empty-state icons, pulse badges are now orange-gradient squares with glow + inner highlight, exactly like the mockup's icon containers.
- **Trend pills** — every ▲/▼ delta is now a soft green/red pill badge (mockup's "+12.5% vs Apr" chips).
- **Tabs & segmented controls** — active segments (Day/Week/Month, analytics tabs, calendar views) are filled with the brand gradient + white text.
- **KPI/stat cards** — layered raised surfaces, tabular numerals, hover lift with orange border glow.
- **Tables** — rounded containers, sticky refined headers, soft orange row hover; status badges became soft pills.
- **Modals/drawers** — header sheen, footer separation, rounded slide-overs with deep shadows.
- **Skeletons** — branded shimmer; **empty states** — dashed premium cards.
- **Forms** — orange accent checkboxes/radios, focus rings, brand text selection; consistent page-title typography on every page.
- **POS tiles, calendar events, class cards** — same hover-lift card language as the dashboard.

**Charts (all of them, zero page-code changes):** a global Chart.js theme now applies the moment the library loads — Inter typography, dark rounded tooltips with orange border, circular legend dots, smooth 0.4-tension curves, rounded bars, subtle grid, refined animations. Every chart on dashboard + analytics picks this up automatically.

**Honest caveats:** I can't render a browser here, so this shipped on verified selectors, not eyeballs. And a handful of bespoke pages (settings' huge form, kpi-bonus, washout) have heavy inline styles that global rules only partially reach — they'll be *much* closer now, but may not be perfect.
